title: saGraph - Samera2022
content: saGraph — a dependency-aware desktop task widget What it issaGraph is a cross-platform desktop widget (Windows and Linux) that keeps your todo list and its task-dependency graph on the desktop. It is not another checklist app; the point is expressing what blocks what, then seeing the whole structure at a glance.Your data stays on your machine. No account, no sign-in, no sync server. What it doesLives on your desktop. An always-present panel, pinnable and draggable, with collapsible category groups. Click a task to toggle it done or not done.Handles dependencies properly. A task’s prerequisite is a boolean expression over other tasks, supporting AND / OR / NOT and any nesting. Empty And([]) is vacuously true, empty Or([]) is false, and no prerequisite counts as satisfied, so both simple and complex conditions express cleanly.Survives cycles. Evaluation carries a visited-stack, so a cyclic chain fails safe instead of recursing forever. You can write a cycle by hand; saGraph will not hang because of it.Draws the graph. A standalone window renders the whole dependency graph and lets you edit it by dragging and connecting, instead of reasoning about dependencies from a flat list.Edits in its own windows. Adding, changing and deleting tasks, categories and dependency expressions happens in a dedicated editor, so editing does not fight with the always-on panel.Stays quiet. Follows the system light and dark theme, starts on boot, enforces a single instance, and sits in the system tray. How it comparesMost task managers treat dependencies as an afterthought, if they support them at all. Todoist has basic blocking. Asana and Monday add dependencies but keep them inside a web app with accounts, seats and subscriptions. Most desktop todo widgets are a list pinned to your wallpaper, with no notion of ordering at all.saGraph makes the dependency graph the main object. List-first appsWeb project toolssaGraphDependenciesBasic or noneYes, but web-boundFirst-class, with AND / OR / NOTGraph viewRareBoard or timelineAn interactive DAG windowOn your desktopSome widgets, no depsNoPanel and graph, always presentAccountUsuallyYesNoDataTheir cloudTheir cloudYour machine, local JSONCyclesUnhandledUnhandledExplicit, fails safeThat leaves a tool that answers two questions the others do not: what you can do right now, and why something is stuck. Paid featureThe dependency-graph window is the first paid feature, gated at runtime rather than by hiding a button: LicencePERSONAL / COMMERCIAL / ENTERPRISETerms1M / 3M / 6M / 1Y / LIFETIMETrialOne 7-day local trialA signed activation code binds the licence to a machine code. The client verifies it with RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 and SHA-256, and stores it AES-GCM encrypted. State is explicit: NOT_VERIFIED, VALID, EXPIRED, INVALID, TRIAL, TRIAL_EXPIRED. When an integrity probe fails, the app degrades softly: free features keep working, paid ones decline. Stack Framework: Tauri 2.x (Rust and Web), one codebase for Windows and Linux Frontend: TypeScript, Svelte, Vite, Tailwind CSS Graph: Cytoscape.js with dagre layout Storage: local JSON behind a Repository trait, with timestamped backup rotation, ready to swap for SQLite or cloud sync later sagraph-core is pure Rust with no Tauri and no platform APIs. Dependency algebra, unlock rules and CRUD live there, and the platform shell is a thin wrapper, so a future CLI, mobile or web build will not need a rewrite.

title: saMacros - Samera2022
content: Samera2022/saMacrosWaiting for api.github.com...00K0K0KWaiting... saMacros — a scriptable desktop automation platform What it issaMacros is the successor to MouseMacros, rebuilt from scratch. It started as a recorder: capture clicks and keys, play them back. Version 3.0 makes a recording the starting point rather than the whole tool.Everything runs locally. No account, no cloud service, no JVM. What it doesRecords and replays. Captures mouse movement, clicks, wheel and keyboard events, then plays them back with timing you control down to the millisecond.Builds flows visually. A block editor assembles automation without code: sequences, if / else, while, repeat, variables, wait until, sub-flows, break / continue, comments. The layout follows the logic, so a flow reads the way it runs.Scripts in JavaScript when you need it. The visual editor has a ceiling; JavaScript does not. The API reads pixel colors, the cursor position and virtual screen bounds, types text, fires notifications, and listens for application events, so a script can respond to what is on screen rather than replaying a fixed tape.Reads the screen. Native sensors expose screen and window state to both the block editor and scripts. A macro can branch on what it sees instead of running blind.Stays out of the way until you call it. Global hotkeys, pause and resume mid-run, and a tray icon. Every hotkey is remappable.Speaks seven languages. English, Simplified Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Russian, Spanish and French, loaded from JSON language packs.Takes plugins. Plugins declare hard or soft dependencies, and a whitelist controls what a script may do. How it comparesMacro tools fall into two camps. Free recorders are simple, usually a click loop and little else. The capable tools either make you learn a scripting language before anything useful happens, or keep the good parts behind a subscription.saMacros is built to sit between them. Simple recordersScript-only toolssaMacrosGetting startedRecord, then playWrite code firstRecord, then playComplex logicNot supportedSupported, steep curveBlocks or JavaScriptScreen awarenessRareManualBuilt-in sensorsPriceFree, limitedSubscriptionOne-time activationRuntimeVariesOften heavyOne native executableAgainst the tools you are most likely to compare it with: TinyTask, GS Auto Clicker, OP Auto Clicker are small, free, and good at a pure click loop. They stop where saMacros starts: no conditions, no variables, no branching, no scripting. AutoHotkey is powerful, free, and the reference point for scripting-based automation. It is a programming language, though, so there is no visual editor and screen reading means writing ImageSearch and PixelGetColor calls by hand. Commercial macro recorders are polished and often good, but usually subscription-licensed, closed, and heavier than a single executable. Game macro tools are frequently ad-supported or bundled, with the trust problems of a third-party download site. The goal is that a beginner records a working macro in under a minute, and a power user grows that same macro into branching, screen-aware, event-driven logic without switching tools. ActivationPaid licensing runs through a separate Cloudflare deployment, not only inside the app: Frontend: an activation page where you enter the machine code and receive a code Backend: a Pages Function that signs the activation with RSA-SHA256 Storage: Cloudflare KV keyed by order, which prevents replay by construction Codes run 1M / 3M / 6M / 12M / lifetime, each bound to one machine code. Stack Language: Rust workspace, GUI in eframe + egui Scripting: rquickjs (QuickJS) Input: direct Win32 calls Release: cargo build --release produces a single saMacros.exe i18n: JSON language packs
